text: Cameron County says just four projects, two LNG export terminals, SpaceX's Starbase and a new shipyard, add up to more than forty-one billion dollars in investment. Some regional tallies go past a hundred billion.

And yet, in the three months through September, the Rio Grande Valley lost jobs. The Dallas Fed says employment here fell at an annualized rate of about six tenths of a percent, roughly seven hundred jobs, while Texas and the country still grew.

That's the puzzle for anyone building here right now. The money is real, but the paychecks haven't caught up, and where they show up first decides where demand for homes, rentals and stores shows up next.
So is the boom real, where is it actually landing, and what should builders, buyers and lenders watch before twenty twenty-seven? This is RGV News.

Start with the money. Cameron County's economic development office lists its four biggest projects as Rio Grande LNG, Texas LNG, SpaceX's Starbase operations and Saronic's Port Alpha shipyard. By the county's own figures, Rio Grande LNG alone is about thirty-two billion dollars.

But those projects are at very different stages. Rio Grande LNG is under construction: its developer, NextDecade, says the first two trains were about eighty percent complete in September, and it expects its first LNG in the second quarter of twenty twenty-seven.

Texas LNG has pushed back its final investment decision for two years running. And Saronic's shipyard won a ninety-five percent county tax abatement in June, with the phases tied to that deal starting in twenty twenty-nine.

So when you hear a number like a hundred ten billion dollars for the region, remember what it is: a tally of projects that are underway, approved or simply announced. It's not money that has already been spent, and it's not paychecks that have already been written.

Now look at the jobs. Earlier this year, the Valley was still adding them: about one point four percent annualized in the first quarter and one point three in the second. In the third quarter, that flipped to a decline.

And the two halves of the Valley are moving in opposite directions. Over the year through October, the McAllen metro added about forty-five hundred jobs, mostly in health care and education. The Brownsville metro, the home of the LNG and SpaceX boom, lost about three hundred.
In the third quarter alone, the Dallas Fed says Brownsville's employment shrank at an annualized rate of almost three percent, while McAllen still grew a little.

Here's the part that's easy to misread. Unemployment actually fell, to six percent in Brownsville and five point eight in McAllen, against four point four statewide. But the Dallas Fed notes that part of that drop comes from a shrinking labor force. In Brownsville, the labor force is down about two percent from a year ago.
A falling jobless rate usually sounds like good news. Here, some of it simply means fewer people are working or looking for work.

So why isn't all that investment showing up in payrolls? This month in McAllen, Dallas Fed senior business economist Luis Torres told Valley business leaders that the weak hiring says more about the supply of workers than about a weak economy.
He said labor force growth has been flat or even negative, that immigration policies have kept some workers without U.S. citizenship out of certain industries, and that wage growth is still solid.

The numbers back him up. The Valley's economy grew about two point six percent in twenty twenty-five, but jobs grew just two tenths of a percent. The Dallas Fed calls it a low-hire, low-fire economy, where output rises without much new hiring.

And pay is still the lowest in Texas. In twenty twenty-five, the median annual wage in the workforce area covering Hidalgo and Starr counties was about thirty-six thousand dollars, the lowest in the state. Cameron County was second-lowest, at about thirty-seven thousand. Statewide, it was about forty-eight thousand six hundred.

The big projects also hire on their own clock. As we covered in Episode 3, Rio Grande LNG was approved for a peak of about seventy-five hundred construction workers, but expects about seven hundred permanent jobs once it runs. Saronic says its shipyard could create up to ten thousand jobs, over a decade.

There are also cracks worth watching. Two Valley trucking companies, Xoco Transport of Hidalgo and American Petroleum Carriers of McAllen, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in recent weeks, and three more carriers filed in Laredo.

Court records show steep drops in revenue and heavy debt on their trucks, and the report points to immigration changes, record diesel prices and a sluggish economy. Across the Valley, business bankruptcies doubled last year, from sixty-two to a hundred twenty-seven.

And this week, a new risk reached the ranches. Texas animal health officials confirmed New World screwworm in cattle in Hidalgo County on November twenty-first, then in Cameron County, and put parts of Cameron, Hidalgo and Willacy counties under animal movement restrictions.
For ranch land and the lenders behind it, that's a new line on the risk list, at least until the quarantine lifts.

Not everything is slowing. Valley cities collected about six percent more sales tax over the year through October, so shoppers are still spending, though those numbers lag actual sales by about two months.

If you build, price for when workers arrive, not when projects are announced. In McAllen, demand is following health care and education jobs now. In Brownsville, it's tied to project timelines: first LNG in the second quarter of twenty twenty-seven, and Saronic's phases from twenty twenty-nine.

If you lend, look hard at freight and trucking borrowers, at ranch exposure inside the screwworm zone, and at rental demand built around construction crews that will shrink once the LNG plant is running.

And watch the calendar. The Dallas Fed updates its Texas jobs forecast every month, first gas is expected at Rio Grande LNG before the end of this year, and Pharr is moving to add three hundred eighty-four acres near its international bridge to its tax reinvestment zone by the end of December.
The boom is real on paper. The question for the next twelve months is how much of it turns into paychecks here. This is RGV News. This video is for information only and isn't financial advice.
The Rio Grande Valley has more than forty-one billion dollars in projects on the books, and it still lost about seven hundred jobs last quarter.
Brownsville's unemployment rate just fell to six percent, but part of the reason is that fewer people are working or looking for work.
The McAllen metro added forty-five hundred jobs in a year. Brownsville, home to the LNG and SpaceX boom, lost three hundred.
Two Valley trucking companies just filed for bankruptcy, and Valley business bankruptcies doubled last year.
The Valley's economy grew two point six percent last year, but jobs grew just two tenths of a percent. Here's why.
